extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century London readers interested in manners, education, and literary taste
extracted.subtask_description: Short Spectator essays giving prescriptive commentary on social behaviour, education of youth, and what constitutes literary genius; intended as practical moral instruction and taste-making for contemporary readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Woman's Man — dress and manner
rubrics_metrics.description: The Woman's Man's garb is more loose and negligent, his manner more soft and indolent; an apparent endeavour to appear unconcerned and careless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and explanation: this studied negligence and unconcern is part of his art to attract women; analogous to a fowler imitating birds to catch them. The text emphasises external affectation (loose dress, soft manner) as deliberate traits that recommend him to the fair sex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Woman's Man — conversational imitation and officiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: He has a similitude of the creature he hopes to betray in his conversation; is very knowing in all that passes from one family to another, has little pretty officiousnesses, and is not at a loss what is good for a cold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: small helpful services and family-knowledge are tools of seduction; keeping a bottle of spirits in his pocket for sudden indisposition is given as a practical advantage. The passage portrays these as tactical accomplishments rather than virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Woman's Man — singularities that recommend him
rubrics_metrics.description: Some singularity in behaviour or whim — what would make him ridiculous among men — recommends him to the other sex; e.g., quarrelling impertinently for their sakes, dressing unlike the rest of the world, or assiduity about the fair sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: the essay argues that affectation, singular habits, and visible devotion (even if insipid) win favour; such eccentricities differentiate him from ordinary men and attract attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Woman's Man — reputation of being with other women
rubrics_metrics.description: He must have the reputation of being well with other women to please any one woman of gallantry; a general fame for falsehood in this kind is a recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: women seek to 'gain slaves from the dominion of others'; the coxcomb loaded with favours is received like a victor. The text notes spite and rivalry among women make a man more desirable if he is popularly favoured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Woman's Man — wit, humour, and inconstancy
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'pleasant thief' is inconstant, has a wonderful deal of wit and humour, never wants something to say, and has a spiteful dangerous tongue if provoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: verbal facility and entertaining speech are more important than constancy or moral worth; these traits make him successful despite moral failings. The essay holds entertainment value above fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Woman's Man — physical marks (strutting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Marks of the Woman's Man: an elevated chest, a pinched hat, a measurable step, and a sly surveying eye — in short, Strutting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: These observable physical habits are presented as reliable signs that a man has ruined many a fair one; any one such feature can undo thousands. The passage warns readers to be wary of such ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of male company women prefer (regular visitants vs ruiners)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular visitants are volunteers admitted on public days to relieve a woman's time; 'ruiners of ladies' are accomplished, informed about court and town, publicly decent but privately dissolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: the essay ranks male company types and commends 'ruiners' as the choicest spirits — accomplished at gossip and public breeding though immoral — because they supply entertainment and social currency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good breeding / decorum — consider time and place
rubrics_metrics.description: Time and place are to be much considered in all our actions; behaviour at church and in other public moments must observe decency (no giggling during sermon, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a tea-table correspondent requests essays 'wholly writ upon good Breeding' and recounts gigglers at church who disturb decency; suggestion that churchwardens enforce behaviour. The guidance urges outward restraint appropriate to setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education — consult natural disposition (indoles)
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural disposition to any particular art, science, profession, or trade (indoles) is very much to be consulted in the care of youth and studied by men when forming schemes of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: illustrated by historical examples (Alexander, Cassius, Scipio) where natural bent predicted future greatness. The essay criticises one-size-fits-all schooling and urges teachers/parents to discern and cultivate native talents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education — avoid universal classical training; match schooling to capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: It is erroneous to force all children through the same great-school curriculum; many excellent tempers are unfit for Aristotle, Tully, or Virgil and should be steered to mechanic trades without respect to birth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: practical recommendations: examine a child's capacity early, dismiss 'honest heavy lads' from slavish schooling sooner, and place them in trades where nature designed them. The essay frames this as a remedy for wasting or degrading children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education — oppose corporal punishment (lashes) as a training method
rubrics_metrics.description: Educating by the lash spoils a child's spirit; corporal punishment reduces a child below the existence of a rational creature and kills native virtue and curiosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: vivid examples of children kneeling, weeping, and becoming debased; the essay argues shame and honour are sufficient regulators and that beating produces ferocity, not true learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of 'bona indoles' in animals and humans
rubrics_metrics.description: There is right value set upon natural strain ('bona indoles') in animals — breeding and natural talents in horses are carefully advertised and prized — a parallel for valuing natural talents in humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: the text prints an advertisement about an honest thoroughbred horse pedigree as an instance of society's proper valuation of native quality; implication: similar care should be paid to human dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes a great genius — natural force vs artful polish
rubrics_metrics.description: A great genius is one who, by mere strength of natural parts and without assistance of arts or learning, produces works delightful in their time and wondrous to posterity; contrasted with the French 'bel esprit' refined by conversation and reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Homer and many ancients are cited as 'natural Genius's' with noble wildness; Shakespear (Shakespeare) is offered as an instance. Guidance warns that imitating the irregularities of such geniuses by rule (e.g., artificial Pindaricks) is ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius should not be imitated by rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Men of sober and moderate fancy should not imitate the extravagant irregularities of natural geniuses; following irregularities 'by rule' produces monstrous compositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: the essay ridicules those who 'strain after the most unbounded flights of Nature' by mechanical arts; cites Pindar and the practice of 'Pindaricks' as examples to be mocked, advising taste and discernment rather than mechanical copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern nicety (bienséance) as corrective to force without correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule of observing 'bienséance' (decency/nicety) in allusion and comparison has been found out in latter years and colder regions to correct the ancients' occasional indecencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: this is presented as a balancing principle — modern writers compensate for less raw force by careful correctness of comparison and allusion; prefer decency where ancients were grand but sometimes indecent.
